lead: A magnetic circuit is the path that magnetic flux takes through iron and air. A coil with N turns and current I supplies a magnetomotive force F = NI. The iron and air oppose flux with reluctance R = l/(μA). The result is Φ = F/R, the magnetic form of Ohm's law. Motors, transformers, relays, inductors and door sensors use this model. It lets you find flux from coil data and geometry before using a field solver.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law and the series and parallel resistor rules, and SI units of length and area.

blocks.text: A coil on a core drives flux round the core. The magnetomotive force (MMF) is F = NI. N is the number of turns, a count. I is the coil current in ampere (A). F is measured in ampere-turns (A·t), often written simply as A. MMF drives flux Φ through the magnetic path. Φ is the total magnetic flux in weber (Wb).

The path opposes flux. Reluctance is R = l/(μA). l is the mean path length in metre (m). A is the cross-sectional area in square metre (m²). μ is the permeability of the material in henry per metre (H/m). Permeability is μ = μ₀μ<sub>r</sub>, where μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m is the permeability of free space. μ<sub>r</sub> is the dimensionless relative permeability. For air, μ<sub>r</sub> = 1. For iron, μ<sub>r</sub> is hundreds to thousands.
Here φ is flux in Wb; F is MMF in A; R is reluctance in A/Wb; N is turns; I is current in A; l is path length in m; A is area in m²; μ is permeability in H/m.

Flux density B is flux per area: B = Φ/A, in tesla (T). The material links B to the magnetic field strength H by B = μH, with H in ampere per metre (A/m). In one uniform path of length l, H = NI/l. In a path made of parts (iron plus an air gap), each part has its own H = B/μ, and the MMF equals the sum of the drops: NI = H₁l₁ + H₂l₂ + …. The same reluctance gives the coil inductance L = N²/R (see self and mutual inductance).

sections.h3: Series paths, parallel paths and air gaps

blocks.text: In a series magnetic circuit, the same flux passes through every part. The core, the air gap and any other section carry Φ. Reluctances add: R<sub>total</sub> = R₁ + R₂ + ... . Then Φ = F/R<sub>total</sub>. A common case is an iron core with one air gap: R<sub>total</sub> = R<sub>core</sub> + R<sub>gap</sub>.

In a parallel magnetic circuit, two or more paths share the same MMF between the same two points. Flux divides: Φ<sub>total</sub> = Φ₁ + Φ₂ + ... . Reluctances combine like parallel resistors: 1/R<sub>eq</sub> = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... . Use this for a core with a side limb or a shunt path.

An air gap has μ<sub>r</sub> = 1, so R<sub>gap</sub> = l<sub>g</sub>/(μ₀A). Even a gap of 1 mm can have reluctance comparable to a metre of iron, because μ₀ is very small and iron μ<sub>r</sub> is large. The gap often sets the flux. Ignore fringing, the spreading of flux at gap edges, and saturation, the fall of μ<sub>r</sub> at high B, unless the question states them.
Here l<sub>c</sub> is core length in m; l<sub>g</sub> is gap length in m; A is area in m²; μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m; μ<sub>r</sub> is relative permeability; R is in A/Wb.

items: Electric and magnetic circuits differ. Current is a flow of charge; flux is not a flow of anything.
Energy is needed to set up flux but not to hold it steady; a steady current in R dissipates I²R all the time.
Resistance hardly changes with current, but μ falls as the iron saturates, so reluctance depends on B.
Air is a good electric insulator but a fair magnetic conductor, so leakage flux has no easy cure.

spec.aria: A rectangular iron core with a coil of 500 turns and a 1 millimetre gap, and its equivalent circuit: an MMF of 1000 ampere-turns driving 0.279 milliweber through the core reluctance 1.59 million and the gap reluctance 1.99 million ampere-turns per weber.

examples.question: A ring core has mean core length 0.4 m, cross-section 4×10⁻⁴ m² and relative permeability 500. It has an air gap of 1 mm. The coil has N = 500 turns and carries I = 2 A. Ignore fringing and saturation. Find the core reluctance, gap reluctance, total reluctance, MMF, flux and flux density. Use μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.
steps: Given: l<sub>c</sub> = 0.4 m, A = 4×10⁻⁴ m², μ<sub>r</sub> = 500, l<sub>g</sub> = 1 mm = 1×10⁻³ m, N = 500, I = 2 A, μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.
Series total: R<sub>total</sub> = R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>g</sub> = 1.59×10⁶ + 1.99×10⁶ = 3.58×10⁶ A/Wb.

Check by MMF drops: H<sub>core</sub> = B/(μ₀μ<sub>r</sub>) = 0.698/(6.283×10⁻⁴) = 1111 A/m, drop 1111 × 0.4 = 444 A; H<sub>gap</sub> = B/μ₀ = 5.56×10⁵ A/m, drop 5.56×10⁵ × 10⁻³ = 556 A; 444 + 556 = 1000 A = NI.
Coil inductance: L = N²/R<sub>total</sub> = 500²/(3.58×10⁶) = 0.0698 H, about 70 mH.
examples.answer: R<sub>c</sub> = 1.59×10⁶ A/Wb, R<sub>g</sub> = 1.99×10⁶ A/Wb, R<sub>total</sub> = 3.58×10⁶ A/Wb, F = 1000 A, Φ = 2.79×10⁻⁴ Wb, B = 0.698 T; the 1 mm gap takes 556 A of the 1000 A, and L ≈ 70 mH.
examples.check:
import math
mu0=4*math.pi*1e-7
l<sub>c</sub>=0.4
A=4e-4
mur=500
l<sub>g</sub>=1e-3
N=500
I=2
R<sub>c</sub>=l<sub>c</sub>/(mu0*mur*A)
R<sub>g</sub>=l<sub>g</sub>/(mu0*A)
Rt=R<sub>c</sub>+R<sub>g</sub>
F=N*I
Phi=F/Rt
B=Phi/A
print(f'{R<sub>c</sub>:.3g}')
print(f'{R<sub>g</sub>:.3g}')
print(f'{Rt:.3g}')
print(F)
print(f'{Phi:.3g}')
print(f'{B:.3g}')

examples.question: A three-limb core has the coil on the centre limb: length 0.1 m, area 8×10⁻⁴ m², with a 0.5 mm air gap. Each outer limb has length 0.3 m and area 4×10⁻⁴ m². μ<sub>r</sub> = 1000 for the iron. Find the current in a 500-turn coil that gives 1 mWb in the centre limb. Ignore fringing and leakage.
steps: Each outer limb: R = 0.3/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 4×10⁻⁴) = 5.97×10⁵ A/Wb. The two are in parallel: 5.97×10⁵/2 = 2.98×10⁵ A/Wb.
The centre limb is in series with that pair: R<sub>total</sub> = 9.95×10⁴ + 4.97×10⁵ + 2.98×10⁵ = 8.95×10⁵ A/Wb.
By symmetry each outer limb carries 0.5 mWb; B = 10⁻³/(8×10⁻⁴) = 1.25 T in the centre and 0.5×10⁻³/(4×10⁻⁴) = 1.25 T in each outer limb.
examples.answer: I ≈ 1.79 A; each outer limb carries 0.5 mWb, and B = 1.25 T everywhere in the iron.

traps: Air-gap reluctance uses μ₀ alone, not μ₀μ<sub>r</sub>. Iron uses μ₀μ<sub>r</sub>. Swapping them is the most common unit-and-physics slip.
Convert every length to metre before dividing. 1 mm = 1×10⁻³ m and 1 cm = 1×10⁻² m. Mixing mm with m² gives a reluctance off by 1000.
The analogy is not identity. MMF is not voltage, flux is not current, and reluctance is not resistance. Only the algebraic rules carry over.

In series, the same flux passes through all parts, so reluctances add. In parallel, the same MMF appears across the branches, so reluctances combine reciprocally and the fluxes add. In a three-limb core the two outer limbs are in parallel with each other and in series with the centre limb.
Saturation and fringing are ignored unless stated. Do not change μ<sub>r</sub> mid-problem or add extra gap area without being told.

quiz.q: Define magnetomotive force and give its unit.
quiz.a: F = NI, where N is turns and I is current in A. Unit: ampere-turn (A·t), often written A.

quiz.q: Write the reluctance formula for a uniform magnetic section and name each symbol.
quiz.a: R = l/(μA). l is length in m, A is area in m², μ is permeability in H/m, R is in A/Wb.

quiz.q: Why can a 1 mm air gap have reluctance comparable to a long iron core?
quiz.a: Air has μ<sub>r</sub> = 1, so R<sub>gap</sub> = l<sub>g</sub>/(μ₀A). μ₀ is very small; iron has μ<sub>r</sub> in hundreds or thousands. The gap length is small but μ₀ is about 10⁻⁶ H/m, so R<sub>gap</sub> is large.

quiz.q: A core has l = 0.5 m, A = 2×10⁻⁴ m², μ<sub>r</sub> = 1000, N = 200 and I = 1 A. No air gap. Find R and Φ.
Two parallel magnetic paths have R₁ = 2×10⁶ A/Wb and R₂ = 4×10⁶ A/Wb. The MMF is 600 A. Find total flux and each branch flux.
State the magnetic Ohm's law analogy in one line.
quiz.a: MMF F ↔ voltage V; flux Φ ↔ current I; reluctance R ↔ resistance R; Φ = F/R ↔ I = V/R.

quiz.q: A ring has R<sub>core</sub> = 1.0×10⁶ A/Wb, R<sub>gap</sub> = 3.0×10⁶ A/Wb, N = 400 and I = 1.5 A. Find Φ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical magnetic design adds fringing, saturation and leakage flux; finite-element software solves the field when the simple reluctance model is too rough. Electric vehicle motors and wireless chargers use laminated cores and ferrites chosen for high μ<sub>r</sub> and low loss. Search terms: magnetic equivalent circuit, Hopkinson's law, fringing flux, B-H curve and finite-element magnetostatics.
